title: Some Stars Get Shredded Again and Again — and Keep Coming Back
hook: A star that survives a dive past a supermassive black hole comes back for another pass, flaring each time. In some systems the flares dim every return, and fast stellar spin may be why.
key_points: A close pass can strip part of a star instead of destroying it — a partial tidal disruption.
The survivor stays in orbit, so the flare repeats every time it returns to the black hole.
In some systems each successive flare is fainter than the last, which needs explaining.
Researchers propose the captured stars were already spinning extremely fast.
Rapid rotation could explain both the fading flares and how the stars reached such tight orbits.
content_html: A star that wanders close to a supermassive black hole does not always get destroyed. If the pass is a near miss rather than a direct plunge, the black hole's tidal pull peels off only part of the star's outer layers — a partial tidal disruption. The survivor stays in orbit, so the flare is not a one-time event: it comes back every time the star does.
extra_html: Astronomers have now found several such systems, and ScienceDaily reports a puzzle inside them: in some, each successive flare is dimmer than the one before. The researchers' proposal is that these stars were already rotating extremely fast before the black hole captured them. Rapid spin puffs a star out and loosens its grip on its own outer layers, which could explain the progressive dimming, and it may also be a clue to how the stars reached such extraordinarily tight orbits in the first place. Repeating flares are valuable precisely because they can be followed: each return is another measurement of the same star being slowly taken apart.

related.hook: A supermassive black hole was caught 30,000 light-years off-centre in its galaxy — it only gave itself away by tearing apart a passing star.

related.title: Black Holes
related.hook: A black hole is a place where gravity wins so completely that nothing — not even light — can escape once it crosses the edge called the event horizon.

related.title: Gravitational Waves: Ripples in Spacetime
related.hook: When black holes collide, they shake the fabric of spacetime itself, sending out ripples that stretch and squeeze everything they pass — by less than the width of a proton.

flashcards.prompt: Why can a tidal disruption flare repeat on a schedule?
flashcards.back_html: If the pass only strips part of the star, the survivor stays in orbit and flares again each time it swings back past the black hole.

flashcards.prompt: What explanation do researchers offer for flares that get fainter with each return?

choices.text: The captured stars were already spinning extremely fast before capture
The black hole loses mass between passes
The flares are actually unrelated background supernovae

flashcards.explanation_html: Rapid pre-capture rotation is the proposed key: it can account for the fading pattern and for how the stars ended up in such tight orbits.

flashcards.prompt: What does a repeating flare tell you that a one-off flare cannot?
flashcards.back_html: That the star was not destroyed. The repetition proves a survivor is still in orbit, and the changes between flares track how it is being worn down.
